newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Health claims sweeten sales but may be hard to swallow.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Health claims sweeten sales but may be hard to swallow.

text.p: Gayle Gilman sat over breakfast in a cafe, studying the label on a jar of raspberry jam as if she were reading the fine print of a tax form.

"I look at the calories and fat but I have no idea what everything else means," the 33-year-old film producer said, referring to the "Nutrition Facts" label now required on nearly every box, bottle and bag of U.S. food.

It's no wonder consumers are confused. With the modern supermarket resembling the local pharmacy, selling products that promise to lower cholesterol, boost energy and maintain blood sugar levels, consumers are left to sort through aisles of confusing and often conflicting information.

The Food and Drug Administration added another ingredient to the mix when it ruled in January that makers of oat products could claim the soluble fiber in oats may help lower the risk of heart disease. Previously the FDA had sanctioned health claims only for food compounds such as calcium or general diets such as low-fat, and health experts expect the latest decision to spark a feeding frenzy as other manufacturers, seeking to boost sales, vie for a piece of the trend linking diet to disease.
"There is a fair amount of evidence that suggests health claims do sell products," Alan Levy, head of the consumer studies branch of the FDA, said.
Indeed, Quaker Oats said the ruling will help maintain the five percent rise in sales of hot cereals reported for 1996.

"We would expect the news surrounding the health claim on oatmeal to continue that momentum," spokesman Ron Battrell said. He said sales of hot cereals including oatmeal reached about $400 million last year.

But while claims may sell products, health experts said, they also send the misleading message that food alone can prevent disease. "It's the quick-fix approach and that's not what healthy diets are about," Marion Nestle, head of New York University's nutrition and food studies department, said.

Moreover, the FDA does not prohibit companies from touting the benefits of oats in foods that contain only trace amounts of the food, along with less-healthy ingredients. Consumers may see the claim on a bag of oat bran pretzels, for example, although pretzels are generally high in salt.
"We are afraid the FDA opened up a can of worms," Bruce Silverglade, an attorney who tracks health labeling issues for the consumer advocacy group Centre for Science in the Public Interest, said.
The FDA denies it has eased the way for a deluge of claims since the application requires widespread scientific proof.

"The number of claims could increase," Ed Scarborough, director of the FDA office of food labeling, said. "On the other hand, there are not many substances or nutrients whose relationships to disease is thoroughly studied."

Scarborough said Kellogg's was seeking permission to use a claim that links psyllium, a type of fiber, with lower cholesterol levels. Other companies are seeking approval to advertise the cholesterol-reducing aspect of soy, he said.

The FDA allows food manufacturers to make ten different health claims on their labels, including the link between a low-fat high-fiber diet and lower rates of cancer and between a low-sodium diet and a reduced risk of hypertension.

Companies that use claims must submit medical studies to the FDA, which conducts an independent review and decides what, exactly, manufacturers may tell consumers. Makers of oats, for example, must say that a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol that includes soluble fiber from whole oats may reduce the risk of heart disease.

While many consumers may not know the difference between saturated and soluble when it comes to breakfast, it is the general message, that a food can have positive effects in the context of a healthy diet, that the FDA hopes to convey.
